title: Why a little Pali
hookLine: a chorus you sing by sound, until you learn what it says
tomorrow: why do chants stretch some sounds and clip others?

lines: A CHORUS YOU SING BY SOUND.
cards: There's a song on your playlist in a language you don't speak. You know every sound of the chorus. You sing it in the car.
Then one day you look up the lyrics, and the next time it plays, the chorus lands differently: you're singing words now, not just sounds. Theravada temples have a chorus like that.
Evening chanting often opens with a line in Pali: namo tassa bhagavato. Some chant it by sound alone, and chant it well.
So, one question for today: if the English is right there, why learn a little of the old language at all?

teach.h: LEARN IT IN YOUR OWN DIALECT.
teach.b: Start with the Buddha's own answer, which is a surprise. In the monks' rule, the Vinaya, two brothers come to him, monks from a brahmin family with fine voices.
Monks from every background are saying his words in their own dialects, they complain, and spoiling them. Their fix: put the teaching into the grand verse of the Vedas. The Buddha says no.
He allows each monk to learn the word of the Buddha in his own dialect. The meaning comes first. So why Pali?

teach.h: PALI: WHERE THE MEANING CAME TO REST.
teach.b: Because the meaning came to rest somewhere. The Theravada keeps its canon in Pali, and its temples chant in it, so two people who share no other language can share one homage. And a few words open the chant from inside.
You already know one. Dhamma: the teaching, the way things are, the first half of the Dhammapada's name.
Pali says dhamma where Sanskrit says dharma. Jewish neighbors know this pull between old words and plain ones.

teach.h: HEAR, O ISRAEL, IN ANY LANGUAGE.
teach.b: The Shema opens, in the JPS 1917 English, "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one."
The Mishnah says the Shema may be said in any language. Shared ground: both let the meaning come in your own tongue, and both keep an old one that lets strangers say the same line together.
One honest difference: the Shema speaks to a people about God. The Pali homage honors a teacher who woke up, and no creator is being addressed.

how: In Theravada temples, monks and lay people chant the homage, the refuges and the precepts in Pali, often with the meaning printed beside it or said after it in the local language.

o: a sacred alphabet kept only by monks in robes
the language of the Theravada canon and its chants
the old name of the land where the Buddha lived

games.q: the words behind the chants — tap the pairs.
p: the language of the Theravada canon

s: Pali is the language of every Buddhist scripture
it's the language of the Theravada canon. other schools, as year four showed, read their texts in other languages.
the Buddha turned down putting his words into the verse of the Vedas
in the Vinaya, he let each monk learn the teaching in his own dialect instead.
dhamma and dharma are two different words
one word: dhamma is the Pali form, dharma the Sanskrit.

games.q: you're a guest at a friend's family temple and the evening chant begins. the sheet has Pali on top and English underneath. you've never chanted. what do you do?
o: chant the Pali sounds with everyone, glancing down at the English.
stay silent; chanting words you can't define yet would be fake.
read the English aloud on your own while the room chants Pali.
games.why: the Buddha let the meaning come in your own tongue, so the English underneath counts. the Pali is what lets a whole room say one line together. sound and meaning, side by side.

practice: Say it out loud, slowly: Pali. Then: dhamma. Say the pair three or four times, letting each word land, the way you'd practice a new friend's name, then sit and let the last sound fade into the quiet.
